To address this, we introduce the Multi-view Oriented Observation (MOO) dataset, a large-scale synthetic AG-ReID dataset of $1,000$ cattle individuals captured from $128$ uniformly sampled viewpoints ($128,000$ annotated images). Using this controlled dataset, we quantify the influence of elevation and identify a critical elevation threshold, above which models generalize significantly better to unseen views. Finally, we validate the transferability to real-world applications in both zero-shot and supervised settings, demonstrating performance gains across four real-world cattle datasets and confirming that synthetic geometric priors effectively bridge the domain gap. Collectively, this dataset and analysis lay the foundation for future model development in cross-view animal ReID. MOO is publicly available at https://github.com/TurtleSmoke/MOO.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 31 pages, 10 figures, extended version of the paper accepted to the CVPR 2026 Workshop on Computer Vision for Animal Behavior Tracking and Modeling (CV4Animals)

Artificial Intelligence.title: Can Linguistic Reasoning Vectors Enhance Multimodal Reasoning Ability?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Most Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are built by extending pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) with visual modules and multimodal alignment. However, this multimodal scaling often degrades the language-side reasoning ability originally encoded in the base LLM. While the base LLM retains usable reasoning after scaling, the aligned VLM itself cannot reliably access this ability. Therefore, recovering the degraded reasoning capability in VLMs would benefit more from seeking help from the base LLM than from the VLM alone. Motivated by this, we propose LIFT (Language-side reasonIng Facilitation and Transfer), a lightweight vector-intervention method that transfers reasoning capability from the base LLM to the VLM without retraining the backbone. LIFT defines Reasoning Vectors as answer-token hidden-state differences between a Reasoner path with an explicit reasoning trace and a Solver path without it, and injects these vectors into language-side activations of the target VLM. LIFT further supports learnable vector adaptation while keeping the VLM backbone frozen. We evaluate LIFT on two VLMs across six reasoning benchmarks, comparing Reasoning Vectors extracted from the base LLM and from the aligned VLM under matched protocols. Results show that LLM-derived vectors consistently outperform VLM-derived vectors, confirming that the base LLM is a more effective source for recovering reasoning. LIFT partially recovers degraded reasoning through lightweight language-side interventions. Further analyses show that Reasoning Vectors influence intermediate reasoning behavior rather than merely altering final answers. The source code will be released soon.

Artificial Intelligence.title: RIVER: Evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval for enzyme--reaction discovery
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Enzyme function annotation and the identification of candidate enzymes for a given reaction are essential steps in connecting genomic information to biochemical reaction networks. However, existing methods rely on sequence or structural similarity or on training with known enzyme--reaction pairs, making it difficult to integrate biochemical evidence across large candidate spaces; they also struggle with retrieval tasks involving enzyme families whose members are highly similar. Here, we introduce RIVER (Reaction--enzyme Inference via Evidence-guided Retrieval), a multi-agent framework for bidirectional enzyme--reaction retrieval that identifies potentially catalyzed reactions for a given enzyme and ranks candidate enzymes for a given reaction. RIVER coordinates large language models, specialized biochemical computational tools, and external knowledge resources to assemble evidence at multiple levels, including reaction chemistry, protein sequences and domains, catalytic mechanisms, and database annotations. Dedicated validation modules further examine evidence gaps and potential conflicts and rerank candidates using traceable evidence records. On public benchmarks, RIVER achieves the highest success rates in both enzyme retrieval and enzyme annotation. In family-specific enzyme retrieval, RIVER outperforms the evaluated baselines on the selected datasets and metrics. In Escherichia coli enzyme retrieval tasks constructed from recent literature, RIVER achieves the best retrieval results with closed-source and open-source model configurations, substantially outperforming closed-source general-purpose and biology-specialized multi-agent systems, including Claude Code, Codex, and Phylo Max. These results suggest that evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval can prioritize biochemically supported enzyme--reaction relationships, providing a basis for subsequent experimental validation.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Scaling Laws for SAE Training Data
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Activation storage is often a bottleneck in sparse autoencoder (SAE) training. We study how many unique activations an SAE needs when its total training budget is fixed. Quality improves rapidly as the buffer grows, then reaches a plateau where replaying the buffer is nearly as effective as using fresh activations throughout training. Beyond this point, additional unique activations bring little benefit to reconstruction or interpretability, so the buffer need not grow with the training budget. We describe this tradeoff between diversity and repetition with a scaling law for limited data. We validate it across dictionary sizes and token budgets, early, middle, and late layers of Llama-3.1, Qwen3 model sizes, and BatchTopK, TopK, and JumpReLU SAEs. Sweeps using mathematical text and Python code test the effect of changing the activation source. Evaluation covers explained variance (EV), reconstruction MSE, feature absorption, automated interpretability, and sparse probing. These results give a practical training rule: choose the smallest buffer that reaches the quality plateau and replay it for the remaining budget. In our experiments, this reduces activation storage by $8\text{--}64\times$ with negligible quality loss.

Artificial Intelligence.title: MedZERO: Self-Evolving Agents for Open-Ended Medical Reasoning Through Controlled Knowledge Accumulation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in medical question answering and clinical reasoning, yet their improvement remains constrained by static parametric knowledge and costly expert supervision. Self-evolving agents offer a promising alternative by enabling models to improve through iterative task generation and problem-solving. However, most existing self-evolving methods are designed for easily verifiable domains such as mathematics and coding, where solutions can be checked by exact answers or executable programs. Medical reasoning is fundamentally different: it is open-ended, knowledge-intensive, and often only partially verifiable. We present MedZERO, a self-evolving framework for open-ended medical reasoning. MedZERO couples an Examiner that generates frontier medical question-option pairs with a Reasoner that solves them through evidence-grounded multi-turn reasoning with external knowledge tools. To support reliable, continual improvement, MedZERO adopts controlled knowledge accumulation, which maintains temporary exploratory knowledge and curated persistent knowledge in reasoning. We evaluate MedZERO on five public medical reasoning benchmarks using 4B- and 8B-scale base models under open-ended evaluation. At both model scales, MedZERO achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated methods. Code is available at https://github.com/IcecreamArtist/MedZERO.

Artificial Intelligence.title: The Unsampled Truth: Quantifying Prompt Artifacts in LM Psychometrics
Artificial Intelligence.summary: When prompting language models for psychometric assessment, researchers assume that the responses reflect the injected persona and the meaning of the survey item. We test this premise using a diagnostic design that crosses five semantically distinct baseline personas with five semantically equivalent variants of each of four prompt components (persona wording, task instruction, item wording, option symbol). Measuring the 1-Wasserstein distance between the resulting response distributions and partitioning the variation among the five components allows for the separation of target effects from prompt artifacts. We apply the framework to 13 open-weight small language models (0.6B to 14B) on the Big Five Inventory and the Short Dark Triad. We find that in most models, the task instruction and option symbol displace response distributions further than paraphrasing the persona description or the item itself. For a substantial share of items, the artifact share of explained variation exceeds 50%; non-semantic changes of the prompt account for more response variation than the baseline personas. Our framework lets researchers quantify these prompt artifacts before interpreting psychometric output.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Accepted to the Findings of EMNLP 2026, Budapest, Hungary

Optimization and Control.title: An Accelerated Proximal Gradient Method for Bures-Wasserstein Space
Optimization and Control.summary: We study composite optimization over the Bures--Wasserstein (BW) space of Gaussian measures. Our main observation is that a useful class of BW problems can be lifted into the Euclidean space of affine transport maps, such that the lifted problems can be solved efficiently using accelerated proximal gradient methods. For objectives whose smooth and nonsmooth components admit convex smooth and convex proximable affine lifts, respectively, our algorithm BW-FISTA achieves minimax-optimal objective gap $O(k^{-2})$ after $k$ iterations. We verify these regularity conditions for potential and interaction energies together with common spectral regularizers, and we treat stochastic gradients under a suitable noise model. As a principal application, we consider Gaussian variational inference with a log-concave, log-smooth target. Here, the resulting entropy term is handled by an efficient, exact proximal step, and we improve the previous rate of $O(k^{-1})$ to $O(k^{-2})$. We numerically verify this predicted boost with synthetic experiments.
Optimization and Control.comment: Submitted on September 2 to the Geometric Distributional Deep Learning workshop at NeurIPS 2026, accepted

Optimization and Control.title: Adversarial Training with Large Step Sizes: Implicit Bias, Optimization, and Sharpness
Optimization and Control.summary: Adversarial Training (AT) is an important method for improving model robustness. We study the dynamics of deterministic Gradient Descent (GD) in AT. Most existing works in this direction focus on the small or vanishing step sizes regime, where GD resembles a continuous-time flow. However, such step sizes can make training inefficient and are rarely used in practice. In this paper, we study the AT dynamics of GD with large constant step sizes. We first study GD in adversarial linear logistic regression, focusing on two aspects: where the model parameters converge (implicit bias) and how quickly the losses decrease (optimization). We then turn to neural networks training and study how the sharpness of losses evolve during AT. Our results advance the understanding of the behaviors of GD with large step sizes in AT and highlight three key differences from its behavior in Standard Training (ST): (i) the implicit bias gap between AT and ST, previously established only for small step sizes, persists for arbitrarily large constant step sizes, (ii) different from ST, there is no uniform rate of convergence for the optimization error in AT, and (iii) sharpness can exhibit two-stage dynamics that differ from the Edge-of-Stability behavior observed in ST.

Optimization and Control.title: Augmented Lagrangian methods with telescopic subproblems for MPCCs and cardinality constraints with general constraints: constraint-preserving swaps and B-stationarity
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider optimization problems with general equality and inequality constraints and partitioned cardinality constraints, which include complementarity constraints. In the augmented Lagrangian method that we consider, the bounds and the cardinality constraints are kept in the subproblems, which are solved by the Telescopic Method. The limit points of this method are B-stationary, without constraint qualifications, if the penalty parameters remain bounded, but not in general. The reason is that the swaps of the Telescopic Method pass through points at which the constraints have different values, and the corresponding variation of the penalty term grows with the penalty parameter. With unbounded penalty parameters and a derivative test outside the current face, the feasible limit points at which a linear independence constraint qualification holds are M-stationary for MPCCs. We modify the swaps, by means of a scaled Newton restoration, so that they preserve the values of the constraints, and we prove that every feasible limit point at which this constraint qualification holds is then B-stationary (S-stationary for MPCCs), whatever the behavior of the penalty parameters. Counterexamples show that the modification is necessary, even with exact solutions of the subproblems, and that the constraint qualification cannot be weakened to one of Mangasarian-Fromovitz type. In the MacMPEC collection, the method found certified S- or B-stationary points in 185 of the 193 instances, more than Algencan and the regularization method of Scholtes. In experiments with cardinality-constrained portfolios and sparse principal component analysis, the constraint-preserving swaps improved the original swaps and the methods applied to complementarity reformulations.
Optimization and Control.comment: 41 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Supplementary material (results by instance) in the ancillary file bmalmpcc-suppl.pdf

Optimization and Control.title: Bridging Batch and Streaming Estimations to System Identification under Adversarial Attacks
Optimization and Control.summary: System identification in modern engineering systems faces emerging challenges from unanticipated adversarial attacks beyond existing detection mechanisms. In this work, we obtain a provably accurate estimate of the Markov parameter matrix of order $k$ to identify partially observed linear systems, in which the probability $p$ of having an attack at each time is smaller than $0.5$. We show that given the batch data accumulated up to time $T^*$, the $\ell_2$-norm estimator achieves an error with stepwise exponential decay as the attack probability $p$ decreases. Furthermore, low-dimensional attack structures can decouple the exponential decay order from the attack probability $p$, achieving an error decay that scales with $T^*$. We then propose a stochastic projected subgradient descent algorithm on streaming data that produces an estimate at each time $t<T^*$, in which case the expected estimation error proves to be the larger of $\mathcal{O}(k/\sqrt{t})$ and the baseline error of the $\ell_2$-norm estimator at $T^*$. This stochastic approach illustrates how non-smooth estimators can leverage first-order methods despite lacking recursive formulas. Finally, we integrate batch and streaming estimations to recover the Hankel matrix using the appropriate estimates of the Markov parameter matrix, which enables the synthesis of a robust adaptive controller based on the estimated balanced truncated model under adversarial attacks.

Optimization and Control.title: A Theoretical Analysis of a Bilevel Optimization Formulation for Combined Local-Global Optical Flow Models
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper analyzes a bilevel formulation for learning the regularization parameter of combined local-global (CLG) optical flow models. The lower-level problem computes the flow from a Lucas--Kanade data term and a quadratic or total variation (TV) regularizer, and the upper-level problem selects the parameter that minimizes the squared distance to a ground-truth flow. The setting is finite-dimensional, and a full-rank assumption makes the lower-level solution unique. For the quadratic model we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of an optimal parameter, for every optimal parameter to be positive, and for strict local optimality. For TV regularization an optimal parameter always exists, because the lower-level solution vanishes for large parameters, and we give a sufficient condition for positivity that accounts for the coupling of the two flow components through the local structure tensors. Synthetic examples illustrate the conditions, including cases in which they fail.
Optimization and Control.comment: 31 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to the Journal of Mathematical Imaging and Vision. Python code in the ancillary files

Optimization and Control.title: Beyond Maximum Likelihood: Variational Inequality Estimation for Generalized Linear Models
Optimization and Control.summary: Generalized linear models (GLMs) are fundamental tools for statistical modeling, with maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) serving as the classical approach for parameter inference. While MLE performs well for canonical GLMs, it can become computationally challenging in more general settings with non-canonical, non-smooth, or saturating link functions, where the resulting optimization landscape may be ill-conditioned, non-convex, or non-differentiable. In this paper, we study an alternative estimation framework based on variational inequalities (VIs), which formulates GLM estimation through an operator-based equilibrium condition rather than likelihood minimization. We analyze the VI estimator from a statistical perspective and establish finite-sample error bounds and asymptotic normality, together with convergence guarantees for fixed-point and stochastic approximation algorithms. The framework accommodates a broad class of link functions, including non-canonical, non-smooth, and non-monotone cases satisfying a strong Minty-type condition, and extends naturally to generalized additive models (GAMs) via basis expansion. Numerical experiments demonstrate that under a fixed iteration budget, the VI approach achieves competitive estimation accuracy and faster, more stable convergence than MLE, particularly in GLMs and GAMs with non-canonical or non-smooth link functions.

Optimization and Control.title: Hardness of integer linear feasibility with cyclic support
Optimization and Control.summary: We prove that integer linear feasibility is strongly $NP$-complete even when the constraint matrix has exactly two nonzero entries in every row and column, with its support forming a single cycle. This holds already for monotone systems (one positive and one negative coefficient in each inequality) with nonzero coefficients of absolute value $2$ or $3$ and right-hand sides in $\{-1,0,1,2\}$. No variable bounds are supplied separately from the system. For systems in which each inequality involves at most two variables, this strengthens known hardness results by restricting all numerical data to fixed finite sets. For systems in which each variable occurs in at most two inequalities, this establishes, to the best of our knowledge, the first $NP$-hardness result for feasibility. We also give negative answers, unless $P=NP$, to questions on polynomial-time solvability of integer programs with bounded coefficients and bounded totally $Δ$-modular treewidth, and on fixed-parameter tractability of integer bound propagation with respect to coefficient and right-hand-side magnitudes.

Optimization and Control.title: Residual-based error control for neural Galerkin reconstruction of minimum-norm wave controls
Optimization and Control.summary: We analyse how errors in independently approximated adjoint waves propagate into the Hilbert Uniqueness Method (HUM) reconstruction of the minimum-$L^2$-norm interior control of a variable-coefficient wave equation. The central result is an identity: the error of the control assembled exactly from any approximate adjoints splits orthogonally into the distance of the minimum-norm control to their observation span and a moment-inconsistency term generated by their interior wave residuals. From it we derive a posteriori bounds for the returned control, including assembly and solve errors, and a continuous accept-or-refine test for the network directions returned by training; under continuous observability, a fully discrete estimate separates truncation, adjoint and assembly errors. The adjoints are computed here by adaptive Galerkin neural networks, but the bounds apply to any computed adjoints. In one-dimensional benchmarks with known minimum-norm controls, all inputs are enclosed by ball arithmetic. Without truncation the residual bounds exceed the true error by factors of 9 to 115; with sixteen adjoints outside the trial class, a truncated terminal space and all inputs computed from the target data, by about 1.08 to 6.50. In two and three dimensions, including a time-dependent coefficient, the neural controls closely reproduce reference controls of the same truncation, and at equal neuron counts trained hidden features reduce the error more than tenfold relative to random features. Classical solvers are much cheaper in all tested cases, and certification is confined to the one-dimensional benchmarks.

Optimization and Control.title: Dynamic Optimistic Constrained OCO with Memory via Delay Equivalence
Optimization and Control.summary: Online Convex Optimization with memory and time-varying constraints (COCO-M) is a recently-introduced framework that captures the dynamics of stateful online learning and non-stochastic control with budget constraints. Despite its expressive power, COCO-M remains largely understudied. In this work, we tackle this problem in its full scale, providing an optimistic algorithm that incorporates untrusted predictions to tame universal dynamic regret and cumulative constraint violation. Our analysis leverages a potent reduction from memory to delay and treats state-dependent gradients as delayed feedback. We establish the first bounds that adapt to both environment non-stationarity (path length $P_T$) and prediction accuracy, while lifting previous restrictive assumptions such as functional separability. En route to these results, we derive findings of independent interest for the memory-to-delay reduction, and for delayed OCO with time-varying constraints. The proposed framework ensures sublinear worst-case guarantees that improve with prediction accuracy, reaching $\mathcal O(1)$ regret under perfect predictions, with cumulative constraint violation (CCV) $\mathcal O(\sqrt{T})$ for unknown $P_T$ and $\mathcal O(\log T)$ for known or online observable $P_T$ , while recovering the optimal COCO rates when memory disappears.
Optimization and Control.comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Optimization and Control.title: A Proximal Newton Framework with Local Superlinear Convergence for Simple Bilevel Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: In this paper, we study a penalty method for simple bilevel optimization in which the lower-level objective has a convex composite structure. Our approach is based on a vanishing-penalty reformulation, which gives rise to a sequence of penalized problems as the penalty parameter decreases. A key difficulty is that metric subregularity of the lower-level optimality mapping does not, in general, yield a uniform error bound for the penalized problems as the penalty parameter vanishes, preventing a direct application of standard proximal Newton theory. To address this difficulty, we first analyze a regularized proximal Newton step by exploiting the specific structure of simple bilevel problems, and establish the local estimates that underpin superlinear convergence. Building on this local analysis, we propose SiB-Newton, which incorporates the proximal Newton step into a globalization strategy. We establish convergence guarantees for SiB-Newton and show that, under suitable local conditions, Newton steps are eventually accepted and the iterates converge at a superlinear rate. Numerical experiments on synthetic examples verify the predicted local superlinear convergence rate.

Optimization and Control.title: Global $\mathcal{O}\left(k^{-2}\right)$ Convergence of Multilevel Gradient-Regularized Newton Methods
Optimization and Control.summary: We develop and analyze multilevel gradient-regularized Newton methods for unconstrained convex optimization with Lipschitz-continuous Hessians. By computing Newton corrections in lower-dimensional subspaces, the proposed methods aim to reduce computational costs while preserving the global $\mathcal{O}\left(k^{-2}\right)$ convergence rate in function values of the full-space method. To establish this rate for multilevel methods, we introduce a class of row-nested restriction operators that ensures monotonicity of the reduced-gradient norms across levels. Numerical experiments with row-nested operators demonstrate convergence behavior comparable to full-space gradient-regularized Newton, while offering substantial computational savings on large-scale instances.

Optimization and Control.title: All minimum cuts of symmetric submodular functions
Optimization and Control.summary: We compute Cunningham's canonical decomposition of a symmetric submodular function on $n$ elements in $O(n^3)$ time. The decomposition represents all minimum cuts in linear space. For the pair $s,t$ produced by Queyranne's algorithm, we construct in $O(n^2)$ time a digraph representing exactly the minimum $st$-cuts of the function. Using this construction in Chekuri and Xu's decomposition algorithm gives the cubic bound.

Optimization and Control.title: G-ORACLE: A Fast Geometric Method To Explore All Near-Optimal Designs for Energy Systems
Optimization and Control.summary:
Modeling to Generate Alternatives (MGA) methods explore the near-optimal solutions of energy system optimization models (ESOMs), i.e., alternative planning pathways whose cost lies within a small predefined slack of the optimum but which can differ substantially in technology composition, regional distribution, and environmental impacts. Among MGA methods, ORACLE uniquely guarantees convergence to the near-optimal set within a targeted tolerance by iteratively refining inner and outer polytope approximations. At each iteration, given a trial point, it solves a problem as hard as the ESOM to find the nearest near-optimal solution to it. However, the trial point is obtained by solving a bilevel problem whose solution time grows rapidly with the number of iterations and eventually dominates the computational cost of the method.
  To eliminate this bottleneck, we present G-ORACLE, which exploits the fact that an optimal solution of the bilevel problem is always attained at a vertex of the outer approximation. G-ORACLE therefore replaces the bilevel problem with incremental vertex enumeration and one convex projection per vertex, while retaining the convergence guarantee of ORACLE. A supporting-hyperplane check further avoids unnecessary recomputation of these projections as the inner approximation grows.
  We evaluate G-ORACLE on an electricity-only PyPSA-Eur model, exploring the near-optimal space of the installed capacities of six generation and two storage technologies. While ORACLE's bilevel problem exceeds 8 hours at iteration 94, G-ORACLE with the beneath-and-beyond method performs the trial-point search in at most 7 seconds throughout 247 iterations, leaving the ESOM solves as the only significant computational cost.

Optimization and Control.title: PPO in the Fisher-Rao geometry
Optimization and Control.summary: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is widely used in reinforcement learning due to its strong empirical performance, yet it lacks formal guarantees for policy improvement and convergence. PPO's clipped surrogate objective is motivated by a lower bound on linearization of the value function in flat geometry setting. We derive a tighter surrogate objective and introduce Fisher-Rao PPO (FR-PPO) by leveraging the Fisher-Rao (FR) geometry. Our scheme provides strong theoretical guarantees, including monotonic policy improvement. In the direct parametrization setting, we show that FR-PPO achieves sub-linear convergence, and for parametrized policies we further obtain sub-linear convergence up to the compatible function approximation error. Finally, although our primary focus is theoretical, we also demonstrate empirically that FR-PPO can be implemented as a drop-in replacement for PPO and achieves performance comparable to PPO across a range of standard reinforcement learning tasks.

Optimization and Control.title: Viscosity-variational inequality solutions of fully nonlinear second-order stationary mean field games with nonseparable and nondifferentiable Hamiltonians
Optimization and Control.summary: We analyse stationary fully nonlinear uniformly elliptic second-order mean field games with nonseparable and nondifferentiable Hamiltonians by introducing the notion of viscosity-variational inequality solution. In this formulation of the problem, the value function is the viscosity solution of the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation, and the Kolmogorov--Fokker--Planck (KFP) equation for the player density is understood as a nonstandard variational inequality that no longer involves partial derivatives of the value function. The advantages of this formulation are found in its stability and continuity properties for handling weak convergence arguments, which we use to prove the existence of solutions of the problem. Furthermore, we prove the equivalence of the notion of viscosity-variational inequality solution with the notion of a partial differential inclusion solution, where the value function is a strong solution of the HJB equation and the player density is a very weak solution of the KFP equation with coefficients belonging to subdifferential sets of the Hamiltonian. Finally, we prove the uniqueness of solutions in the case of separable Hamiltonians with strictly monotone couplings.

Optimization and Control.title: Mirror Descent-Ascent for mean-field min-max problems
Optimization and Control.summary: We study two variants of the mirror descent-ascent (MDA) algorithm for solving min-max problems on the space of measures: simultaneous and alternating. We work under assumptions of convexity-concavity and relative smoothness of the payoff function with respect to a suitable Bregman divergence, defined on the space of measures via flat derivatives. We establish non-asymptotic convergence rates to mixed Nash equilibria, measured in the Nikaidô-Isoda error, proving an $\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})$ rate for simultaneous MDA and an improved $\mathcal{O}(N^{-2/3})$ rate for alternating MDA. The main technical contribution is an infinite-dimensional dual space analysis that relates Bregman divergences on measures to dual Bregman divergences on spaces of bounded continuous functions, allowing us to control asymmetric commutator terms created by alternating updates. The results substantially generalize prior analyses restricted to bilinear objectives and also apply to nonlinear convex-concave problems on measure spaces, thereby providing a unified theoretical foundation for MDA in mean-field min-max optimization.

Optimization and Control.title: Exponential Consensus and Flocking in Multi-Agent Systems with Infinite Fading Memory
Optimization and Control.summary: In this paper, we study the emergent collective dynamics of multi-agent systems driven by infinite distributed fading memory of Volterra type. We establish a unified theoretical framework covering both first-order opinion consensus dynamics and second-order velocity alignment flocking kinematics. By introducing Dafermos past-history transformations, the governing integro-differential systems are reformulated into dynamical systems on extended product Hilbert spaces. For first-order dynamics, we prove that fading memory inherently provides a hidden dissipative mechanism, guaranteeing unconditional global exponential consensus with or without instantaneous communication forces. For second-order dynamics, by developing a unified energy-multiplier framework that seamlessly couples instantaneous communication with memory dissipation, we establish unconditional global exponential flocking for both the pure fading memory system and the mixed interaction system, completely independent of the spatial dispersion or the communication tail.

Optimization and Control.title: Worst-Case Finite-Horizon Analysis of Perturbed LQR via Performance Estimation Problem
Optimization and Control.summary: We propose a framework to assess the robustness of a given state-feedback controller by evaluating its worst-case finite-horizon cost over a class of norm-bounded perturbations. To compute this cost, we show how to apply the Performance Estimation Problem (PEP) framework, originally developed to analyze optimization algorithms, and reformulate the worst-case search as a rank-constrained Semidefinite Program (SDP). Our results suggest that the perturbations that induce the highest finite-horizon costs can differ substantially from those identified using standard asymptotic metrics. Intuitively, worst-case perturbations are obtained by aligning slowly decaying modes with specific initial conditions to drive transient growth, causing a bifurcation in the worst-case behavior as the horizon length changes. These findings open new possibilities to certify finite-horizon performance of broader system classes, including data-driven models or nonlinear components.

Optimization and Control.title: Adaptive pairwise preference elicitation for decision support: identifying the best alternative with fewer judgments
Optimization and Control.summary: Interactive decision support systems often require repeated preference judgments, although identifying the best alternative may not justify eliciting all \(n(n-1)/2\) pairwise comparisons. We propose ALEC (Adaptive Lexicographic Elicitation of Comparisons), which re-ranks the alternatives after each judgment and asks the first unobserved pair in the lexicographic order of the current ranking, using the Analytic Hierarchy Process as the concrete setting. Under a log-normal error model, directly comparing a contrast maximises the one-step reduction in its effective resistance. Posterior bounds on the probability of a wrong choice or of exceeding a relative-loss tolerance provide stopping rules valid under adaptive questioning, while a consistency-and-margin condition gives a deterministic certificate of agreement with the full-matrix winner. Simulations show that re-ranking is most useful in larger problems with limited budgets; ALEC outperforms Harker's original rule in most scenarios with \(n\ge11\), while under a common stopping rule it achieves higher hit-rate point estimates than the stronger Harker-log variant at a modest additional questioning cost. With a 5\% loss tolerance and a cap of \(2n\) additional comparisons, the stopping rule saves \res{prot-s06-saveadd-min}--\res{prot-s06-saveadd-max}\% of them, while among runs stopped by the bound the observed rate of losses above tolerance remains at most \res{s06-errearly-max}\%, against a nominal 10\%. ALEC therefore provides an adaptive elicitation module for decision support systems that balances decision precision against user effort.

Optimization and Control.title: Convergence and Stability of a Catching-Up Algorithm for Differential Inclusions with Maximally Monotone Operators
Optimization and Control.summary: We study a catching-up algorithm with approximate projections for finite-dimensional differential inclusions governed by a maximally monotone operator and a continuous perturbation. Through the canonical decomposition of the operator into a regular part and the normal cone to the closure of its domain, the problem becomes a sweeping process, discretized by an explicit predictor step and a feasible approximate projection. For variable time steps, the approximations converge, up to a subsequence, to a solution on every finite horizon when the mesh size and the accumulated projection-error budget vanish and the nodes stay in a common compact convex set. This set comes from linear growth on finite horizons and, without any growth condition, by dissipativity of the projected field at a feasible center, which confines the nodes to a fixed ball uniformly in time for small steps and small projection errors. Under either condition, locally Lipschitz perturbations give global well-posedness, convergence of the whole family, and, for a common initial state, a trajectory-error estimate of order $O(\sqrt{h+E})$, where $h$ is the maximal step and $E$ the accumulated budget; sparse projection errors are allowed. An elastic network with unilateral stops illustrates the results, and numerical experiments compare the algorithm with the full-resolvent discretization.

Optimization and Control.title: Overcoming Fundamental Control Limitations in Powered Descent Flight through Robust Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion
Optimization and Control.summary: This work identifies a fundamental, controller-independent limitation in reusable launch vehicle powered descent: a sudden $180^\circ$ phase transition in the open-loop transfer functions from the control inputs to the lateral drift and drift rate. The transition occurs inside the flight envelope, reverses the effective control direction, and can destabilize the closed loop system under uncertainty. An analytical condition governing this transition is derived, its physical mechanism is established, and its dependence on vehicle mass, aerodynamic properties, and geometry is characterized. An Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion (INDI)-based control architecture is then developed to inherently address this limitation and is tuned via $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ Closed Loop Shaping to provide local robustness and performance guarantees. The internal dynamics introduced by the INDI inversion are analytically derived and proven to be stable throughout the flight envelope. The proposed controller is compared against a robust gain-scheduled baseline controller through linear stability analysis and an extensive nonlinear Monte Carlo campaign. Both controllers achieve 100% success across the considered Monte Carlo campaign, though the INDI-based controller provides improved tracking performance, superior nominal and dispersed stability margins, requires fewer controller design points, and reduces controller tuning complexity.
Optimization and Control.comment: 28 pages, 16 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for presentation at the AIAA SciTech 2027 Forum, Orlando, FL, January 2027

Optimization and Control.title: A two-stage approach to satellite constellation optimization: classical and QUBO formulations
Optimization and Control.summary: The design of satellite constellations for Earth observation requires balancing spatial coverage, revisit time, cost, and operational complexity. This paper considers the problem of designing the orbits of a given number of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) or Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) satellites to maximize the spatial and temporal resolution achieved over a prescribed set of ground targets. This kind of problem is inherently nonconvex and possibly combinatorial, making its solution computationally demanding for large constellations and target sets. To address this challenge, we propose a two-stage optimization strategy that separates spatial-coverage design from temporal-resolution optimization, thereby reducing the complexity of the overall problem. Two variants of the method are developed. The first employs continuous decision variables during the spatial-optimization stage, whereas the second discretizes these variables and reformulates the problem as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem. The latter formulation enables the use of efficient classical QUBO solvers and is directly compatible with quantum-annealing hardware. The proposed framework provides a scalable approach to the design of heterogeneous LEO and VLEO Earth-observation constellations and establishes a pathway for exploiting emerging quantum-optimization technologies in satellite mission design. Preliminary simulation results are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the strategy.

Optimization and Control.title: On the Minimal Controllability of Boolean Networks With $k$-Regular Dependency Graphs
Optimization and Control.summary: Boolean networks (BNs) are widely used to model gene regulatory networks and other biological systems. In this paper, we investigate the minimal controllability problem for BNs subject to degree constraints. We first establish three new best-case upper bounds for XOR-BNs whose dependency graphs are $k$-regular. We then introduce classes of BNs that are invariant under cyclically partite transformation (CPT-invariant) and prove theorems connecting BN controllability with the surjectivity of vector-valued Boolean functions. Finally, by combining an analysis of this surjectivity with a probabilistic argument, we derive a new general lower bound on the minimum number of control nodes required for majority-type threshold BNs with $(2k+1)$-regular dependency graphs.

Optimization and Control.title: A Solution Method for Single-Source Capacitated Facility Location Problems Under Decision-Dependent Demand Uncertainty
Optimization and Control.summary: We present a model and an exact solution method for single-source capacitated facility location problems with decision-dependent demand uncertainty. The model allows the joint probability distribution of customer demands to depend on the facility to which demand points are allocated. The number of possible decision-dependent distributions is therefore equal to the number of feasible allocations of demand points to (groups of) facilities. To address the exponential size of the model, we apply and extend a recent version of the L-Shaped method for stochastic programs with decision-dependent uncertainty. In particular,we compare the original optimality cut with a new optimality cut based on a bilinear reformulation. We prove that, separated together with the original one, the new cut yields a tighter restriction, at the expense of introducing bilinear terms. In addition, we prove an effective decision-independent valid inequality that significantly improves convergence. Extensive numerical tests on 180 instances demonstrate that the method, supported by the valid inequality, can find optimal or near-optimal solutions to problem instances with up to 620 potential probability distributions. The tests also show that, while the new cut closes slightly more instances, the original cut remains preferable in terms of solution time and optimality gap.

Optimization and Control.title: A globally convergent stochastic semismooth Newton method for strongly convex problems in Hilbert spaces
Optimization and Control.summary: We propose and analyze a globalized stochastic semismooth Newton method for stochastic optimization problems in Hilbert spaces where the objective is strongly convex with Lipschitz continuous, Newton differentiable gradient. Gradient and generalized Hessian information are only available through mini-batching. In each iteration, a full semismooth Newton trial step is accepted or rejected based on a stochastic residual test and rejected steps are replaced by damped steps in the same Newton direction. Throughout, we admit gradient estimators with affinely growing variance, as arises in optimization problems with random partial differential equations as constraints. We prove non-asymptotic global R-linear convergence in expectation as well as almost sure convergence. For sufficiently fast-growing batch sizes, the method transitions almost surely into a regime of pure Newton steps and converges R-superlinearly almost surely. The method is applied to the optimal control of a random elliptic equation featuring a Huber tracking term as well as a random parabolic equation with a Moreau--Yosida penalization of an almost sure state constraint.

Optimization and Control.title: Fully nonlinear second-order mean field games with nondifferentiable Hamiltonians
Optimization and Control.summary: We analyse fully nonlinear second-order mean field games (MFG) with nondifferentiable Hamiltonians, which take the form of a coupled system of a fully nonlinear Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation and a Kolmogorov--Fokker--Planck partial differential inclusion (PDI) featuring the set-valued subdifferential of the Hamiltonian. We show the existence of solutions of some stationary MFG systems with quite general coupling operators and nonnegative distributional source terms, on general bounded convex domains, under the primary assumptions of uniform ellipticity and the Cordes condition on the diffusion coefficient. The existence proof is founded on an original, and equivalent, reformulation of the PDI as a nonstandard variational inequality (VI), that offers significant flexibility in passages to limits. Furthermore, the uniqueness of the solution of the PDI/VI system is proved in the case of strictly monotone couplings. We then show how the MFG PDI/VI system in the fully nonlinear setting can be obtained as the limit of a sequence of PDE systems with differentiable Hamiltonians, and we give further results on the continuous dependence of the solution.

Optimization and Control.title: Funnel MPC for port-Hamiltonian systems
Optimization and Control.summary: Port-Hamiltonian systems are an energy-based modelling formalism, that has strong ties to the physical models and allows interconnection of systems. Funnel MPC, a Model Predictive Control (MPC) scheme, allows for output tracking with prescribed error bounds. Earlier works focused on systems with stable internal dynamics, which typically excludes port-Hamiltonian systems. We introduce a modified stage cost design that takes into account the port-Hamiltonian structure of the system and allows deactivation of the funnel cost. We show initial and recursive feasibility for a class of port-Hamiltonian systems with relative degree one including unstable internal dynamics.

Optimization and Control.title: Quantifying the remaining search space in analogue optimisation
Optimization and Control.summary: Benchmarking analogue optimisers requires certifying not only how close a returned energy is to the optimum, but also how many better configurations may remain. Semidefinite relaxations provide rigorous bounds on the ground-state energy and selected observables, yet reveal little about the size of this residual search space. We introduce a deterministic, instance-specific upper bound on the number of binary configurations whose energies improve upon a returned state by a prescribed margin. Combined with a semidefinite energy interval, this yields a complementary certificate of both the magnitude and multiplicity of any possible improvement. To judge an analogue optimiser's native performance, we provide a generalisation of the framework to obtain bounds on the Haar volume of the remaining continuous phase-space. To further characterise the remaining search space, we extend our bounds to resolve regions in configuration space in both the binary and continuous setting. Our approach couples a variational-Chernoff reduction with an elimination bound of the resulting partition function. Comparisons with exact enumeration and independent Haar sampling are consistent with the bounds on small instances. In numerical experiments at $N=1000$, even the largest family-median bound restricts the potentially improving binary configurations to less than $10^{-144}$ of the full configuration space, while the largest upper bound on the corresponding Haar volume is of order $10^{-499}$.

Optimization and Control.title: Reversible Dynamics, Asymmetric Actions: Parking as a Trajectory-Level Affordance
Optimization and Control.summary: Drivers are often told to back into a tight parking space, not drive in nose first. The advice looks paradoxical, because a slow car is dynamically reversible: reverse its speed and replay the steering backward, and it retraces a feasible path. Played backward, though, reverse-in shows a car driving forward out of the space. Reverse-in and forward-in are different tasks: they share a start position but end facing opposite ways. We separate three clearances between car and obstacles. Static fit $F$ is the clearance the parked car keeps at its best acceptable destination pose. Eventual access $A_\infty$ is the clearance it can keep all the way there with unlimited corrections. Resource-bounded access $A_K$ is the clearance that survives a budget of $K$ reversals, switches between forward and reverse. They satisfy $F\ge A_\infty\ge A_K$. In one fully specified scene (one car, bay, aisle and start), a certified argument proves $A_\infty=F=0.5000$ m for both tasks. In this scene, all certified forward/reverse asymmetry therefore arises at finite $K$: it lies in how many corrections each task needs, not in the clearance either can eventually keep. With one reversal, an explicit path gives reverse-in at least $0.4410$ m clearance. A certified reachability argument caps forward-in's one-reversal clearance at $d_0<0.1720002$ m. With two reversals, forward-in gets at least $0.2833$ m. To keep a clearance strictly above any $d$ with $d_0\le d<0.2833$ m, reverse-in thus needs exactly one reversal and forward-in exactly two when both tasks move forward first. If both move in reverse first, the counts are two and three. The contrast depends on the start position (Section 4.15). Proposed experiments test whether observers distinguish fit, eventual access and budgeted access. They compare these with simpler cues, such as how the turning body sweeps, and learned manoeuvre labels.

Optimization and Control.title: On the Spectral Dependence of Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Tracking
Optimization and Control.summary: We study how the spectral geometry of the mixing matrix enters the convergence of decentralized stochastic gradient tracking (GT) for smooth strongly convex problems. General bounds contain the factor $Δ_λ^{-3}$ in the higher-order stochastic term, where $Δ_λ$ is the absolute spectral gap. We show that, even for two agents with identical quadratic objectives, the exact steady-state mean-square disagreement scales as $α^2σ^2Δ_λ^{-3}$ as the nontrivial eigenvalue approaches $-1$, provided the stepsize $α$ is sufficiently small relative to the gap. Here $σ^2$ is the gradient-noise variance. By unrolling the disagreement recursion, we establish a stochastic bound that averages all nontrivial eigenvalue contributions for diagonalizable mixing matrices, up to an eigenvector conditioning factor. As a real or complex eigenvalue approaches the unit circle away from $1$, its contribution grows as the inverse cube of its distance to the circle; growth can be slower near $1$. For symmetric mixing with gaps $p$ at $1$ and $ν$ at $-1$, the weighted sum $θ_1/p+θ_2/ν^3$ replaces the prior factor $(Δ_λν^2)^{-1}$. For $N$ agents, $Nθ_1$ and $Nθ_2$ count the nonnegative and negative nontrivial eigenvalues, respectively. On a symmetric family, a finite-horizon lower bound for the average iterate matches the worst-case factor $p^{-1}+ν^{-3}$ up to universal constants. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted scaling.

Optimization and Control.title: XM4D: 4D Reconstruction through Certifiable Geometric Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: Accurate 4D reconstruction remains challenging: jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry, and non-rigid deformation entails highly nonconvex optimization, making global optimality difficult to guarantee. We present XM4D, a framework for accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction built upon certifiably globally optimal geometric optimization. By separating the estimation of camera motion from non-rigid deformation, we formulate both stages as structured quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQP) that admit semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations and verifiable global optimality certificates. For camera motion estimation, we lift static point tracks into 3D using foundational depth prediction models and formulate a scaled bundle adjustment problem that jointly estimates camera poses, depth scales, and static landmarks. By analytically eliminating translations and landmarks, we reduce the problem to a QCQP over scaled rotations. For non-rigid reconstruction, we represent dynamic motion using an embedded deformation graph (EDG) and show that its tracking, rigidity, and temporal regularization objectives similarly reduce to a rotation-only QCQP. Both problems admit SDP relaxations that we solve efficiently with a GPU-accelerated Burer-Monteiro solver based on Riemannian optimization. The recovered geometry further initializes dynamic Gaussian splatting for photometric refinement. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate accurate camera motion estimation on both static and dynamic scenes, efficient optimization that scales to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality.

Optimization and Control.title: Quantifying and minimizing collision intensity in stationary crowd flow
Optimization and Control.summary: We develop a continuum model to quantify kinematic collision risk in stationary crowd flow. From the density-weighted inward relative flux, we derive a collision functional based on the symmetric velocity gradient. For incompressible flows with constant density, this functional is convex and positively homogeneous of degree one in a combination of second derivatives of the stream function. We minimize it subject to prescribed boundary flux. On bounded simply connected domains with Lipschitz boundary, under a finite-energy lifting assumption, we prove existence of minimizers in a relaxed class that allows this derivative combination to be a vector-valued Radon measure. We show that disks are the only domains with a nontrivial zero-trace kernel, corresponding to rigid rotation about the center. Using the compact embedding for functions of bounded deformation, we prove that relaxed energy sublevels are compact without normalization on every other admissible domain, and after removing one rotational component on disks. We identify the relaxed functional with the strong $W^{1,1}$ lower semicontinuous envelope of the functional on the prescribed-trace class with integrable controlled derivatives. Then, we derive optimality conditions via convex duality. We construct explicit radial flows on annular sectors and prove that they minimize the energy over the full admissible classes, including nonradial competitors. On the square, distinct minimizers with the same prescribed boundary flux have different local collision intensities. The square--disk comparison shows that the saddle flow loses optimality when the domain changes, even after normalization.

Optimization and Control.title: On the Rate of Gaussian Approximation for Online Linear Regression Problems
Optimization and Control.summary: In this paper, we consider the problem of Gaussian approximation for the online linear regression task. We derive the corresponding rates for the setting of a constant stepsize and study the explicit dependence of the convergence rate on the problem dimension $d$ and quantities related to the design matrix. When the number of iterations $n$ is known in advance, our results yield a normal approximation rate of order $\sqrt{\log{n}/n}$, provided that the sample size $n$ is large enough.

Optimization and Control.title: Newton Steps are Faster for Linear Complementarity Problems
Optimization and Control.summary:
Linear Complementarity Problems (LCPs) with sufficient matrices form a well-studied class of problems, dating back from the foundational works of Cottle and Dantzig (1968). LCPs capture convex quadratic programs, and admit reductions from problems such as discounted stochastic games or mean-payoff games. While the original approach for solving these problems was based on pivoting methods, in their 1991 book, Kojima, Megiddo, Noma, and Yoshise introduced an interior point method (IPM) with running time that is polynomial in the input size, but which depends linearly on a certain parameter called the handicap number of the matrix. Despite the ensuing rich literature on sufficient LCP IPMs, the linear dependence on the handicap number has not been improved since then.
  We present an IPM whose running time depends on the square root of the handicap number. The algorithm can decrease the duality gap by a constant factor in $O\left(\min\left\{\sqrt{n} (1+κ),n^{9/8}\sqrt{1+κ}\right\}\right)$ iterations. Curiously, this can already be achieved using standard Newton updates. We analyze the IPM in a norm defined by a local weighting, where centralizing Newton steps quadratically converge to the central path, without any dependence on the handicap number. The weights arise from a characterization by Rump (Linear Algebra and Its Applications, 1997, 1998, 2003) of the sign-real spectral radius and its relation to sufficiency; another ingredient of our proof is a new operator norm characterization of the handicap number.
  Moreover, the connection to Rump's work also enables us to show coNP-completeness of testing sufficiency, and approximation hardness of the handicap number.

Optimization and Control.title: Near-Optimal Decentralized Stochastic Convex Optimization over Networks
Optimization and Control.summary: We study decentralized stochastic smooth convex optimization, where $M$ workers minimize an average objective using local stochastic gradients and neighbor-only communication over a fixed gossip network. A central question in this setting is to determine the largest number of workers that can be used under a total budget of $N$ gradient samples while still preserving the centralized $O(1/\sqrt N)$ statistical rate. We introduce an accelerated decentralized method that preserves this rate for up to $\smash{M\lesssim \sqrtρ\,N^{3/4}}$ workers, where $ρ$ is the spectral gap of the gossip network, improving the best prior maximal scaling of $\smash{M\lesssim ρ\sqrt N}$. The method is based on a one-step-delayed stochastic acceleration scheme that enables workers to interleave minibatching with accelerated gossip while controlling residual disagreement, and its guarantee depends only logarithmically on the optimum-local heterogeneity. We also establish a matching lower bound for linear-span decentralized first-order methods, showing that the method is optimal up to logarithmic factors.

Optimization and Control.title: Online Optimization for Controlling HVAC Systems
Optimization and Control.summary: Heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems account for a significant portion of buildings' energy consumption, motivating the design of energy- and cost-efficient control strategies. However, conventional strategies employ simple, reactive control, without incorporating a model. Therefore, in this paper we adopt an economic model predictive control framework and focus on designing online algorithms to solve the control input design problems with a limited computational budget. In particular, we propose two tailored online algorithms based on projected gradient descent, with a custom projection routine, and the projected primal-dual method. We discuss the pros and cons of both algorithm designs, focusing in particular on computational efficiency. We further compare them through numerical experiments simulating the control of an HVAC system over the course of a day. The results show that computationally efficient online solvers for HVAC systems control are indeed possible. Moreover, the performance closely matches that of a baseline algorithm with unlimited computational budget, in terms of reference temperature tracking and comfort temperature range enforcement.

Optimization and Control.title: Grokking or Glitching? How Low-Precision Drives Slingshot Loss Spikes
Optimization and Control.summary: Deep neural networks exhibit periodic loss spikes during unregularized long-term training, a phenomenon known as the "Slingshot Mechanism." Existing work usually attributes this to intrinsic optimization dynamics, but its triggering mechanism remains unclear. This paper proves that this phenomenon is a result of floating-point arithmetic precision limits. As training enters a high-confidence stage, the difference between the correct-class logit and the other logits may exceed the absorption-error threshold. Then during backpropagation, the gradient of the correct class is rounded exactly to zero, while the gradients of the incorrect classes remain nonzero. This breaks the zero-sum constraint of gradients across classes and introduces a systematic drift in the parameter update of the classifier layer. We prove that this drift forms a positive feedback loop with the feature, causing the global classifier mean and the global feature mean to grow exponentially. We call this mechanism Numerical Feature Inflation (NFI). This mechanism explains the rapid norm growth before a Slingshot spike, the subsequent reappearance of gradients, and the resulting loss spike. We further show that NFI is not equivalent to an observed loss spike: in more practical tasks, partial absorption may not produce visible spikes, but it can still break the zero-sum constraint and drive rapid growth of parameter norms. Our results reinterpret Slingshot as a numerical dynamic of finite-precision training, and provide a testable explanation for abnormal parameter growth and logit divergence in late-stage training.

Optimization and Control.title: Randomized and Oracle-Based Feasible Directions Methods for Nonsmooth Nonconvex Constrained Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: Minimizing nonsmooth nonconvex objectives over general convex sets using no derivatives of the objective, together with structural access to the constraint set, poses a fundamental geometric difficulty: at boundary points, the feasible direction cone may fail to be closed, preventing the construction of finite sets of search directions that capture all feasible descent directions. We develop a feasible-directions framework for problems structured as the difference between a continuously differentiable function and a convex function over a closed convex set, and access the objective without knowledge of its decomposition, through exact line searches along feasible segments. To address the geometric obstruction, we introduce $η$-feasible directions, which remain uniformly separated from the boundary of the feasible direction cone, enabling finite-direction search even in the presence of nonlinear constraints. We present two algorithmic realizations of this framework. The first assumes access to an $η$-direction oracle and extends feasible-directions methods from linear to general convex constraints. The second replaces the oracle by a noise-augmented randomization scheme that constructs spanning directions from the affine-hull inner normal and almost surely avoids nonsmooth boundary points when initialized outside that set. Under curvature bounds and Lipschitz continuity of the smooth component's gradient, we jointly control the spanning coefficients and feasible step lengths of the oracle construction. This yields finite-time approximate $d$-stationarity along every unit feasible direction admitting a prescribed positive step length. For both methods, we also establish a rate in the proximal directional minimization (PDM) measure, assuming uniformly bounded direction-set sizes. Randomized exploration ensures that, almost surely, every accumulation point is $d$-stationary.

Optimization and Control.title: Randomized Parallel Complexity of Weakly Convex Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the minimum number of query rounds needed to find approximate stationary points of nonsmooth weakly convex functions, measured by the gradient of the Moreau envelope. Each round permits multiple simultaneous queries. In the stated parameter regime, the standard subgradient rate is optimal in sufficiently high dimensions, even for randomized algorithms making polynomially many parallel queries per round. We then show how the order structure of the real line enables faster search: a deterministic algorithm using only function values achieves logarithmic round complexity, with a further reduction through parallel queries. Matching lower bounds hold even when each query returns the entire subdifferential. Together, these results clarify the role of dimension in determining the benefits of parallel queries for weakly convex optimization.

Optimization and Control.title: A Graph-Theoretic Approach to Matrix AM-GM: Counterexamples and Sharp Exponential Bounds
Optimization and Control.summary: We develop a graph-theoretic approach to the expected-norm matrix arithmetic--geometric mean inequality. By encoding matrix interactions with a path-supported Gram matrix, we obtain a projection family whose product is nonzero exactly when the transition graph of its index sequence is a path. This gives an intuitive explanation for failure: repeated indices can create cycles or branches that annihilate products, an effect absent for positive scalars. We prove the universal lower bound $(n)_m/n^m$ for the ratio of the with-replacement to the without-replacement mean and show that it is asymptotically sharp on the exponential scale when $m=n$. Specifically, our construction gives a ratio $\exp(-n+O(\sqrt n))$, matching the lower bound's leading exponential rate over unrestricted dimensions. We also determine an explicit overlap threshold, derive exact six-factor counterexamples, and show that exponential failure can coexist with vanishing pairwise commutators.

Optimization and Control.title: Projection-Free Gradient Tracking Neurodynamic for Distributed Nonnegative Sparse Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper proposes a continuous-time, projection-free neurodynamic system based on gradient tracking for distributed nonnegative sparse optimization. Unlike traditional methods, our approach avoids projecting states onto the feasible set. Instead, it employs gradient tracking to estimate average gradients under heterogeneous costs, coupling primal and dual dynamics such that feasibility and sparsity emerge naturally from the equilibrium conditions. The system ensures unique solutions through a locally Lipschitz vector field and guarantees that every equilibrium corresponds to an exact KKT point. We establish rigorous convergence guarantees for convex objectives through three distinct analytical layers. These include a centralized kernel rate, a computable distributed rate derived from Jacobian analysis without restrictive stability assumptions, and a global exponential stability proof based on Lur'e system theory. Our analysis quantitatively separates these layers, revealing that the convergence rate is primarily limited by graph sparsity and remains robust to variations in momentum time scales. Numerical experiments on strongly convex quadratic problems validate the theoretical rates, demonstrate effective active set recovery, and show that the system maintains stable tail convergence rates even under strong local heterogeneity.

Optimization and Control.title: A Bilevel Neurodynamic Approach for Distributed SCAD-Regularized Sparse Least Squares
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper proposes a bilevel particle swarm optimization (PSO)-neurodynamic method for solving the distributed sparse least-squares problem regularized by the smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD) penalty to global optimality. The SCAD penalty is nonsmooth and nonconvex, so existing distributed neurodynamic methods have not been extended to it directly. Through two-time-scale singular perturbation analysis, a rigorous full-trajectory convergence theory with explicit convergence rates is established for the inner collaborative multi-agent neurodynamic system without requiring the second-order sufficient condition. A theory-guided inner-outer collaborative optimization framework is further developed, in which a red-light green-light sensitivity mechanism is embedded in the outer PSO search to enhance global search while concentrating computational effort on the SCAD shape parameters, thereby improving recovery accuracy and computational efficiency. Simulation results on four sparse-recovery scenarios demonstrate that the proposed method accurately recovers the true sparsity pattern and achieves faster convergence and lower relative error than competing neurodynamic methods.

Optimization and Control.title: Q-Learning under Finite Model Uncertainty
Optimization and Control.summary: We propose a robust Q-learning algorithm for Markov decision processes under model uncertainty when each state--action pair is associated with a finite ambiguity set of candidate transition kernels. This finite-measure framework enables user-designed uncertainty models, including competing fitted models and stress scenarios. {The learner observes successor states and their deterministic rewards from every candidate simulator, without requiring explicit knowledge of the transition probabilities or the reward function.} We establish almost sure convergence of the learned Q-function to the robust optimum, and derive a time-uniform high-probability error certificate that separates an observable empirical Bellman residual from transition-kernel estimation error. We also give quantitative finite-ambiguity approximation results for Wasserstein and parametric uncertainty models on finite state spaces. Numerical examples illustrate the effect of scenario selection and compare the tabular algorithm with robust value iteration.

Optimization and Control.title: Learning and Steering in Incomplete-Information Games
Optimization and Control.summary: In many modern multi-agent systems, a mediator seeks to influence strategic decision dynamics using only outcome-level feedback and without knowing agents' utilities. In this work, we study how a mediator can learn an unknown game and steer adaptive agents toward outcomes that maximize her utility using only trajectory feedback. The mediator knows the game form and her own objective, but not the agents' utilities. Moreover, she commits to nonnegative payments and provides recommendations and contexts, but receives only a single realized terminal outcome rather than full-information feedback. We develop halving-type algorithms that learn utility differences in normal-form games and conditional continuation-value differences in extensive-form games, achieving a sample complexity of $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ that matches worst-case lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. We then combine these learning procedures with a Lagrangian formulation in an online Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm that interleaves learning, equilibrium computation, and steering toward mediator-optimal extensive-form correlated equilibria (EFCE). With high probability, the Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm achieves a directness gap and an optimality gap of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/4})$, while time-average payments are of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/8})$.

Optimization and Control.title: SAGE: A Set-based Adaptive Gradient Estimator
Optimization and Control.summary: We introduce a set membership perspective on gradient estimation for black-box scalar functions, in which the gradient is not approximated as a single point estimate but characterised as a member of a set of admissible gradients consistent with available function samples and regularity assumptions. Bounds on gradient uncertainty, obtained from standard multivariate Taylor series results, are used to represent this admissible set through linear inequalities, making gradient uncertainty explicit and directly exploitable. Building on this formulation, we propose an adaptive strategy to refine the admissible gradient set to a desired precision by selectively acquiring new samples only when necessary. The resulting framework naturally accommodates function evaluations affected by noise with finite but a priori unknown bounds, yields the theoretical best attainable precision of the gradient set, and provides the optimal sampling distance from the point of interest to maximise information gain during refinement. Within this framework, we introduce the Set-Based Adaptive Gradient Estimator (SAGE), which extracts an estimate of the true gradient from the admissible set whilst preserving high sample efficiency and robustness to noise. Numerical experiments on large collections of random gradient-query points, as well as in the context of a first-order optimisation method, compared the performance of SAGE against commonly used gradient estimators from the literature. Our results show that SAGE achieved competitive gradient accuracy across noise levels without requiring any a priori noise characterisation. In a first-order optimisation setting, noise-informed competitors can outperform SAGE when such characterisation is available. Nevertheless, SAGE remained broadly competitive, making it particularly attractive in settings where noise characterisation is impractical to obtain.

Optimization and Control.title: Distributionally Robust Airport Ground Holding Problem under Wasserstein Ambiguity Sets
Optimization and Control.summary:
We develop a distributionally robust formulation of the single-airport ground holding problem (dr-SAGHP) using a $1$-Wasserstein ambiguity set with an $\ell_1$ transportation metric over the full physical capacity support. We exploit the problem's structural properties to develop an exact dynamic programming separation algorithm within delayed constraint generation (DCG-DP). We also develop K-IL, which combines Kelley's cutting-plane method with an integer L-shaped framework to solve a a restricted-support approximation, rs-dr-SAGHP. Delayed constraint generation with MILP separation (DCG-MILP) serves as the computational baseline. Computational experiments demonstrate substantial runtime reductions for DCG-DP and K-IL relative to this baseline.
  Airport capacity distributions are constructed using Gaussian process regression based on historical weather and operational data at Denver International Airport from 2021 to 2023. We develop a chronological expanding-window calibration procedure to select the Wasserstein radius and the results show that the calibrated dr-SAGHP approaches reduce mean operational cost by approximately $2.6\%$ and the Conditional Value at Risk $\mathrm{CVaR}_{90}$ by approximately $8\%$ relative to the stochastic SAGHP benchmark, while avoiding the excessive conservatism observed in a classical robust optimization benchmark.

Optimization and Control.title: Who pays for urban environment management? The role of the third-party service provider
Optimization and Control.summary: The dominant contemporary paradigm of direct state-led urban environmental regulation entails significant risks, including high administrative burden, frequent conflicts with polluting entities, and economic vulnerabilities for those sources. To address these deficiencies, this paper integrates third-party service provider (TPSP) into China's existing management framework as a beneficial extension beyond conventional government intervention. Utilizing an evolutionary game approach, we compare two distinct institutional settings, a non-integration management mode and an integration management mode, and scrutinize the evolutionary dynamics across both two- and three-dimensional systems. To enhance system robustness, we embed a strategic behavior-based dynamic punishment mechanism that effectively eliminates the perturbing effects of varied penalty rules, thereby steering all stakeholders toward an ideal stable state. This comparative institutional analysis isolates the marginal contribution of third-party intermediation, specifies when outsourcing environmental services outperforms direct government enforcement, and reframes evolutionary game theory as a design device for institutional self-correction. Furthermore, a predefined variable importance analysis is conducted to highlight critical factors warranting attention in practical policy implementation. Extensive simulation experiments, carried out under diverse system-level and parameter-level conditions, validate the theoretical properties of our model. The findings offer concrete managerial insights to inform the formulation of more effective urban environmental supervision regulations.
